content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes to use structural features constructed based on the union subgraph of two nodes as the edge feature between two nodes, to further improve the expressive power of graph neural networks. The paper gives the reasons why it chooses union subgraphs, and why it uses the spectrum of a path-based matrix as the structural feature. Experiments demonstrates the benefits of the adopted structural features.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengthes:
1. The idea to use structural features of a union subgraph of a pair of nodes is new for graph level tasks, although it is not new in general to improve GNN expressive powers. The first works consider injecting structural features into GNNs are [1]. Also, [2] exactly uses the spectral norm of the matrix of shortest-path-length distances as structural features. 

2. The motivations behind different designs are explained very clear and paired with examples. I appreciate this effort. 

3. The types of experiments are extensive, though the used datasets are not representative enough. The experimental results generally show the benefits of the proposed approach. At the beginning, I have some concerns on the computation complexity, while the authors defend themselves well by providing efficiency analysis. 

Weaknesses:
1. My big concern is about the significance of this work. This is another method to outperform 1WL GNN. There have been so many works on this topic. Different works may propose different designs, while how optimal this work is in theory, and why this work is better than others? These are not super clear in this paper. The authors have used a few examples to justify the points, while to me this reads not strong enough. In particular, the method is only provably more expressive than 1WL. How far it can reach is unclear. 

Also, constructing structural features to improve GNN expressive power is not a new idea. The authors miss discussing many works on the similar topics. Here, I just mention three closely related missing references [1,2,3]. [1] is the first work to inject structural features (distance features) to improve GNN expressive power with provable results. [1] originally proposes to use shortest path distances to a pair (or a set) of nodes to define structural features and gives theoretical analysis. [2] uses the spectral norm of the shortest path-distance-defined matrix like the one in this work to define structural features. These works should be discussed. Also,  can the authors provide any quantitive theoretical analysis results like [1] and [3] ([3] also leveraged structural features within a subgraph around each node)? And, can the authors compare the adopted method with more powerful GNNs in theory such as 3WL GNN but not just in practice?

2. Another concern is about the experiments. Different aspects have been evaluated in experiments and this is great. However, since the theoretical contribution is not that sufficient, more challenging datasets and more extensive experiments are expected. For example, most adopted datasets are small. Also, only a subset of OGB graph-level datasets has been used. Also, graph-level regression tasks over datasets such as QM9 have not been used to evaluate expressive power. Typically, I do not ask for these many experiments. However, as the theoretical contribution is not that sufficient, the experiments are expected to be extensive. 

Currently, I giving a marginal recommendation is by assuming that the authors may use more challenging datasets and tasks to evaluate the method. If the authors can indeed provide such evaluations and/or provide a more solid theory for the work, I would like to give a strong recommendation. 


[1] Distance encoding: design provably more powerful neural networks for graph representation learning, Li et al. NeurIPS 2020
[2] Principled hyperedge prediction with structural spectral features and neural networks, Wang et al. arxiv' 2021
[3] Nested Graph Neural Networks, Zhang & Li, NeurIPS 2022

content.title: Response to Reviewer S6Hp
content.comment:
•	[Significance of the Work.] Many thanks for this insightful comment. As discussed in [1], the comparison of the expressive power between different GNN extensions remains an open question. In particular, high-order WL tests are concepts of global comparisons over two graphs. Therefore, it is arguable if the WL hierarchy is a suitable tool to measure the expressiveness of GNN extensions as the latter focus on locality. Nonetheless, there exist some graph structures such that the 3-WL test and GraphSNN are not stronger than UnionSNN, i.e., some graphs can be distinguished by UnionSNN but not by 3-WL and GraphSNN. Similar analyses have been performed in existing works [2, 3]. As an example, UnionSNN can distinguish the 4x4 Rook’s graph and the Shrikhande graph (as shown in Figure 7, Page 15 in our revision), while 3-WL and GraphSNN cannot, which suggests that UnionSNN is stronger than 3-WL and GraphSNN on such graphs. This could be explained by the fact that the number of 4-cycles in these two graphs are different, and UnionSNN is able to reflect the number of 4-cycles with the consideration of $E^{vu}_3$ edges in union subgraphs. We have formulated this analysis in Appendix D in the revision.

•	[Missing References.] Thank you for pointing out these missing references. Our UnionSNN leverages the shortest path matrix to encode substructure information for message reweighting, while DE-GNN uses distance encoding to augment node features and to control the receptive field of message passing. SNALS utilizes an affinity matrix based on shortest paths to encode the structural information of hyperedges. The affinity matrix is designed to measure the connectivity between two hypergraphs (target nodes and their nearby nodes) instead of representing the local substructure itself. NGNN represents a graph by pooling the rooted subgraph instead of the rooted subtree. However, which substructure to choose and how to capture the complete information of local substructures have not been well investigated. Unlike the quantitative analysis in NGNN, we perform a qualitative theoretical analysis in Appendix B.3 to prove that our UnionSNN is strictly more expressive than 1-WL for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. We have added the discussions on the above methods to our related work in the revision (Page 2). We have also included NGNN as a new baseline in our graph classification experiments and reported the results in Table 1. The results show that UnionSNN outperforms NGNN in all cases.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an edge feature augmentation based on distance matrix on edge-enclosing subgraph which is useful to boost MPNN-like architectures on graph and node classification tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

- This papers proposes a feature engineer technique which can be plugged into any MPNN-like achiectures to improve their expressivity for graph and node classification tasks.


## Weakness

The experiment part should be improved.

- From current experiment results, it looks like that your archiecture UnionSNN is not good (nearly half of the cases are not improving), thus I think the outcome here is using your proposed edge feature augmentation can improve performance. However, to show this conclusion, you should thoroughly compare performance of the same MPNN-like architecture with all other substructure descriptors as augmentation methods. I only see such a comparison on GraphSNN which do not always yield best performance, thus it is not enough.
- Besides, your method should work for any MPNN-like architecture, but it is only used for GCN, GIN and GraphSNN, why it is not applied on other methods in Table 1 and 2? I do not see any barricade at least for GAT, GatedGCN and GraphSAGE.
- Is there any theoretical explanation of minus performance over union in Table 3? Since minus is always a subset of union, such behavior is not straight and need explanation.

Another minor concern is why you limit only on node and graph classification. You are utilizing enclosing subgraphs for all edges, and as far as I know, there is work [1] utilziing similar things, but for link prediction.

[1] Chamberlain, Benjamin Paul, et al. "Graph Neural Networks for Link Prediction with Subgraph Sketching." arXiv preprint arXiv:2209.15486 (2022).

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6BpF (1/2)
content.comment:
- [“Complete” and “Best”.] Many thanks for the comment. In our work, we discuss the local structure that represents the relationships between 1-hop neighbors. We restrict the discussion to the 1-hop neighborhood because we aim to develop a model based on the MPNN architecture, in which a single layer of convolution is performed on the 1-hop neighbors. In this regard, the union subgraph we choose is able to characterize the complete picture of the 1-hop neighborhood. For the “best”, we use it to characterize the properties of the substructure descriptor. We list down three desirable properties for distinguishing non-isomorphic substructures and show that the proposed shortest-path-based descriptor satisfies the three properties and meanwhile retains the information of a union subgraph (Theorem 2). We have modified the corresponding places in the revision (Page 4) to avoid overclaims.

- [Definition of “Overlap Isomorphism”] Sorry for the confusion on this concept. The last “isomorphic” in the definition refers to the ordinary “graph isomorphism”. The concept of “overlap-isomorphic” is defined over two subgraphs $S_i$ and $S_j$, where $S_i$ is an induced subgraph of $\tilde{N}(i) = N(i) \cup$ {$i$} (i.e., the 1-hop neighborhood of a node $i$). The bijective mapping $g$ is between the node sets of $S_i$ and $S_j$, i.e., $\tilde{N}(i) $ and $\tilde{N}(j)$. The definition of "overlap-isomorphic" requires that for any $v \in N(i)$, the pair of corresponding overlap subgraphs $S_{i \cap v}$ and $S_{g(i) \cap g(v)}$ are isomorphic (ordinary graph isomorphic), where $g(i) = j$ and $g(v) = u$. Therefore, “overlap isomorphism” is defined based on the ordinary graph isomorphism of any pair of overlap subgraphs, where each corresponding pair is defined based on $g$. Note that when we talk about an “overlap subgraph”, denoted as $S_{i \cap v}$, it refers to a subgraph based on an edge $(i, v)$, and is defined as $S_i \cap S_v$. It contains only edges in $E^{iv}_1$. 

	We give an example for this concept. As shown in the Figure 6, Page 13 in our revision, we have two subgraphs $S_{v_1}$ and $S_{v_2}$. These two subgraphs are overlap-isomorphic. The bijective mapping $g$ is: $g(k_1) = g(k_2)$, $\forall k \in$  {$v, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h$}. Take a pair of corresponding overlap subgraphs as an example: $S_{v_1 \cap g_1}$ and $S_{v_2 \cap g_2}$. They are based on two red edges $(v_1, g_1)$, and $(v_2, g_2)$ and the rest of the edges in the overlap subgraphs are colored in blue. It is easy to see that $S_{v_1 \cap g_1}$ and $S_{v_2 \cap g_2}$ are isomorphic (ordinary one). In this ordinary graph isomorphism, its bijective mapping between the nodes is not required to be the same as $g$, just as in the case of $S_{v_1 \cap g_1}$ and $S_{v_2 \cap g_2}$. It could be the same or different, as long as the ordinary graph isomorphism holds between this pair of overlap subgraphs. In this example, any pair of corresponding overlap subgraphs defined under $g$ are isomorphic (ordinary one). In fact, all overlap subgraphs have the same structure in this example. In this sense, the concept of “overlap isomorphism” doesn’t look at the neighborhood based on a single edge, but captures the neighborhoods of all edges and thus the “overlap” connectivities of the two subgraphs $S_{v_1}$ and $S_{v_2}$. 

	We have added the example in the revision (Appendix A) for better understanding.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6BpF (2/2)
content.comment:
- [Definition of “Union Isomorphism”] The concept of “union isomorphism” is the same as that of “overlap isomorphism”, except that “union subgraphs” are used in place of “overlap subgraphs” as the pair of subgraphs in the ordinary graph isomorphism part.
In the above example subgraphs $S_{v_1}$ and $S_{v_2}$, there doesn’t exist a bijective mapping $g$, based on which the corresponding pairs of union subgraphs are isomorphic (ordinary one). The union subgraph $S_{v_1 \cup k}$ for any $k \in $ {$a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h$} is $S_{v_1}$ itself, and the same for $S_{v_2}$. Since $S_{v_1}$ and $S_{v_2}$ are not isomorphic (ordinary one), these two graphs are not union-isomorphic.

- [Complete Picture of the Neighborhood.] Thanks for pointing out this confusion. We didn’t specify the context clearly in this statement. We mean that the substructures we define by the concept of "union subgraphs" are the largest possible if we consider the 1-hop neighborhood of an edge. We have rephrased the sentence in the Abstract to be more specific. May we ask if there are more doubts after "that it is" in this point?

- [Novelty and Merits.] Many thanks for the comment. We emphasize that, comparing to other subgraph-based approaches and other substructure descriptors (as discussed respectively in Sections 3.2 and 4.1), our method (1) chooses a better local substructure that characterizes the complete 1-hop neighborhood information, and (2) designs a substructure descriptor that meets three desirable properties to guarantee its ability to distinguish non-isomorphic (sub)graphs. We have modified the Introduction to better position our work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new graph neural network model called Union Subgraph Neural Network (UnionSNN), where the core idea is to consider a certain class of subgraphs induced by two adjacent nodes. This model therefore can be seen another example of subgraph-based graph neural networks, which uses shortest path distances as descriptors. Authors show that the model is strictly more expressive than 1-WL, hence surpassing the expressive power of classical graph neural networks. They also conduct an empirical analysis on model variations, including different descriptors, and report their findings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The study of subgraph based aggregation is an important direction, and there is a value in discussing the advantages/disadvantages of different descriptors.

Weaknesses:

- The paper is really hard to follow: The concepts are relatively simple but the writing hinders readability.
- The formal analysis is very limited. Theorem 3 is a straight-forward observation (even, if we were to ignore existing results). It also doesn't tell us anything about the upper bound in the expressive power of UnionSNNs.
- The idea of using shortest paths dates back to shortest path graph kernels, and is also used in multiple recent works authors cite, e.g., SPNs (Abboud et al., 2022), Graphormer (Ying et al., 2021).
- The work is not located well in the existing literature: it is unclear why this model is superior to other subgraph-based approaches, or other shortest-path related approaches. Some of these works are credited in the paper, but there is a lack of discussion in terms of model properties as well as in terms of empirical analysis. The proposed model is a simple extension of GIN which uses the descriptors.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There is significant room for improvement in the presentation. What is the exact motivation of this paper?  How does it compare to existing approaches and what are potential advantages/disadvantages? It is hard for me to answer these questions in the current state of the paper. In my opinion, this paper could be better placed as a review of existing subgraph models using different descriptors and comparing them under different assumptions and on different empirical setups. The proposed models do not appear novel to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is largely incremental on ideas from the literature, but a better framing of the paper may be possible since there are some interesting empirical insights. However, the current state of the paper clearly falls under the acceptance threshold.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1386 by Reviewer 5gGi

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5gGi
content.comment:
•	[Analysis of Expressive Power.] Thank you for the comment. As discussed in [1], the comparison of the expressive power between different GNN extensions remains an open question. In particular, high-order WL tests are concepts of global comparisons over two graphs. Therefore, it is arguable if the WL hierarchy is a suitable tool to measure the expressiveness of GNN extensions as the latter focus on locality. Nonetheless, there exist some graph structures such that the 3-WL test and GraphSNN are not stronger than UnionSNN, i.e., some graphs can be distinguished by UnionSNN but not by 3-WL and GraphSNN. Similar analyses have been performed in existing works [2, 3]. As an example, UnionSNN can distinguish the 4x4 Rook’s graph and the Shrikhande graph (as shown in Figure 7, Page 15 in our revision), while 3-WL test and GraphSNN cannot, which suggests that UnionSNN is stronger than 3-WL and GraphSNN on such graphs. This could be explained by the fact that the number of 4-cycles in these two graphs are different, and UnionSNN is able to reflect the number of 4-cycles with the consideration of $E^{vu}_3$ edges in union subgraphs.  We have formulated this analysis in Appendix D, in the revision.
 
•	[Use of Shortest Paths.] We are not the first to use shortest paths in GNNs. However, our way of using shortest paths is different from recent works discussed in Section 2.2. We use shortest paths to transform an entire local subgraph to a matrix for further edge encoding, while Graphormer encodes the shortest path information to the bias of the softmax attention as spatial encoding and SPN adopts shortest paths to guide the multi-scale graph convolution. In both Graphormer and SPN, only the shortest distances from the central node are taken into account and the distances between neighbor nodes are completely ignored.

•	[Novelty and Presentation.] Many thanks for the comment. We emphasize that, comparing to other subgraph-based approaches and other substructure descriptors (as discussed respectively in Sections 3.2 and 4.1), our method (1) chooses a better local substructure that characterizes the complete 1-hop neighborhood information, and (2) designs a substructure descriptor that meets three desirable properties to guarantee its ability to distinguish non-isomorphic (sub)graphs. We have modified the Introduction to better position our work.

[1] Papp P A and Wattenhofer R. A Theoretical Comparison of Graph Neural Network Extensions[C]// International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR.

[2] Balcilar M, Héroux P, Gauzere B, et al. Breaking the limits of message passing graph neural networks[C]//International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021: 599-608.

[3] Bodnar C, Frasca F, Wang Y, et al. Weisfeiler and lehman go topological: Message passing simplicial networks[C]//International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021: 1026-1037.

[4] Huang Y, Peng X, Ma J, et al. Boosting the Cycle Counting Power of Graph Neural Networks with I $^ 2$-GNNs[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.13978, 2022.
